items.value: People will adopt low-carbon behaviour only if companies and governments incentivise them by making low-carbon options cheaper and more widely available
items.reasoning: The passage's pivot is its last sentence: even the half of the reduction that comes from behavioural change 'would require companies and governments to provide more incentives to change'. That is exactly option B. A is wrong because the passage says household cuts deliver at most half, not that they are the only route. C inverts the passage: supply-side investment is what makes low-carbon options cheaper, not the other way round. D introduces subsidies to manufacturers, which the passage never mentions.

items.value: Only assumption I is valid: supply-side investment by companies can produce low-carbon behaviour in people
items.reasoning: Assumption I is what the passage rests on: incentives delivered 'through supply-side investments to make low-carbon options cheaper and more widely available' are presented as the thing that enables household behaviour to change, so I is valid. Assumption II overstates it into an absolute incapacity claim. The passage says achieving that half of the reduction requires incentives; it never says people are incapable of any low-carbon behaviour on their own. An absolute 'not capable ... without' is not what the text assumes, so II fails.

items.value: A circular economy - recovering and reusing materials - can be beneficial for sustainable growth
items.reasoning: The passage sets out rising raw-material consumption, a reuse rate below 9%, scarce and costly battery metals, and long risky supply chains, and concludes 'Reusing materials makes sense'. The moderate, pragmatic reading of that is C. A ('not possible without'), B ('every sector ... immediately') and D ('the only option') are all absolutes the passage never asserts; the text recommends reuse as sensible, not as the sole or immediate imperative.

items.value: Only assumption II is valid: economic growth is compatible with circular use of mineral resources
items.reasoning: The passage urges reuse on economic grounds - the materials are pricey, hard to obtain and carry supply-chain risk - which presupposes that industry can keep growing while recovering and reusing its materials. So II is a genuine underlying assumption. I is not: the passage says spent batteries 'should go back to a factory', a recommendation about what ought to happen, not a claim that automobile factories already exemplify a circular economy.

Per-pipe rates: X = 0.70/(14 x 20) = 1/400 tank per minute; Y = (3/8)/(6 x 10) = 1/160; Z drains (1/2)/(20 x 16) = 1/640. Open: 10 pipes of X = 10/400 = 1/40, 5 pipes of Y = 5/160 = 1/32, all 16 of Z = -16/640 = -1/40. The X and Z terms cancel exactly, leaving a net 1/32 tank per minute, so 50% of the tank takes (1/2) / (1/32) = 16 minutes.

1^n is always 1. For n = 1, 2^n = 2, so 1 + 2 = 3 leaves remainder 3. For every n greater than or equal to 2, 2^n is divisible by 4, so 1 + 2^n leaves remainder 1. The remainder set is therefore {3, 1}, giving exactly 2 distinct values. (Natural numbers are taken to start at 1, the Indian convention; including n = 0 would add the remainder 2.)

A number of the form QQQ equals Q x 111 = Q x 3 x 37, and 481 = 13 x 37. So the HCF is 37 x HCF(3Q, 13). Since Q is a single digit, 3Q lies between 3 and 27 and 13 can divide it only if 13 divides Q, which no digit does. Hence HCF(3Q, 13) = 1 and the HCF is 37 for every choice of Q from 1 to 9 - checked for all nine values.

Numbers 1 to 9 contribute 9 digits (positions 1 to 9). The 90 two-digit numbers 10 to 99 contribute 180 digits (positions 10 to 189). That leaves 489 - 189 = 300 digits among the three-digit numbers, and 300 = 3 x 100 exactly, so position 489 is the last digit of the 100th three-digit number. That number is 199, whose last digit is 9.

Taking the usual convention for such puzzles - the guilty person's statements are all false and the innocent ones speak the truth - only P works. If Q were guilty, his statement 'R did not steal' would have to be false, making R the thief too, which contradicts there being one culprit. If R were guilty, the innocent P's claim 'Q stole it' would have to be true, again contradicting a single culprit. P guilty is fully consistent: both his statements are false and everything Q and R say is true. Note the stem never states a truthfulness rule, so the item leans on an unstated convention; on a strictly literal reading option D would also be arguable.

items.value: Both statements are correct - P v Q was a 0-0 draw, and R scored 1 goal against Q
items.reasoning: Exhaustive search over all three match scores with each team scoring exactly one goal in the tournament and the points ending 3, 2, 1 gives a single possibility: P v Q drawn 0-0, Q v R drawn 1-1, and P beating R 1-0. Check: P gets 1 + 2 = 3, Q gets 1 + 1 = 2, R gets 1 + 0 = 1, and each side's goals total 1. Since that scenario is unique, statement I (0-0 draw between P and Q) and statement II (R scored 1 against Q) are both correct.

items.value: Relying wholly on genetically refined crops carries a risk of food insecurity
items.reasoning: The passage's argument runs: climate change may make plant infections more common, and centuries of selective breeding have bred the spare genetic variation out of high-value crops - 'good for yields but bad for coping with changes' - so 'a minor disease or even an unknown one could suddenly rampage through a genetically honed crop'. That vulnerability of our narrow crop base is the central idea, which is B. A misplaces the emphasis on productivity when the passage is about disease vulnerability. C is not discussed. D prescribes replacing honed crops with wild varieties, which the passage never proposes.

items.value: Only assumption I is valid: climate change can spread plant diseases into new areas
items.reasoning: Assumption I is directly carried by the line that such changes risk making 'some plant infections more common in all climatic zones' - infections reaching zones where they were not previously common is exactly a migration to new areas. Assumption II brings in wild relatives of crops, which the passage never mentions at all; it speaks only of variation being bred out of cultivated genomes. II is a true-in-the-world claim imported from outside the text, which is the standard distractor in this format.

items.value: The opposition is indispensable in a democracy for balancing political power and securing good governance
items.reasoning: The author says a statesman should 'pray never to be left without opponents; for they keep him on the path of reason and good sense', and closes on national unity depending on 'a sufficiently even balance of political power'. D captures both halves - the indispensability of opposition and the balance of power. A reverses the argument. B is directly contradicted, since the passage wants it to be impracticable 'for opposition to be revolutionary and irreconcilable'. C misreads the point: rulers need opposition's criticism, not its support, and the passage is about good governance rather than political survival.

Assumption I makes opposition conditional on an indifferent head of government; the passage makes it unconditional, saying the statesman should pray never to be left without opponents at all. Assumption II equates aggressiveness with better governance; the passage argues the opposite, wanting a balance even enough to keep the opposition from becoming 'revolutionary and irreconcilable'. Both fail, so the answer is neither.

items.value: Only four statements are definitely true (I, III, IV and VI)
items.reasoning: P is the brother of Q and R, so the three are siblings and P is male; S is R's mother, hence mother of all three; T is P's father, hence father of all three. That makes III (T is Q's father), IV (S is P's mother) and VI (P is S's son, P being male) definitely true, and I true on the standard convention that the father and mother of the same children are a couple. Statements II and V fail on gender: nothing tells us Q or R is male or female, so 'Q is T's son' and 'R is T's daughter' are not definite. Four in all. The one judgement call is statement I; if 'couple' were held to require proof of marriage the count would drop to three.

X does one-third in 6 days, so the whole in 18 days, rate 1/18; Y does one-third in 8 days, so the whole in 24 days, rate 1/24; Z does three-fourths in 12 days, so the whole in 16 days, rate 1/16. Together they do 1/18 + 1/24 + 1/16 = 23/144 per day. Y alone in 8 2/3 = 26/3 days completes (26/3)/24 = 13/36 of the work, so the joint phase covered 1 - 13/36 = 23/36 = 92/144. Then n = (92/144) / (23/144) = 4.

The successive differences are 3-1 = 2, 6-3 = 3, 11-6 = 5, 18-11 = 7 - the prime numbers in order. The next prime is 11, so X = 18 + 11 = 29, and the prime after that is 13, giving 29 + 13 = 42, which matches the printed last term. That confirmation by the given final term is what fixes 29 over the other options.
